title: 30 First-Person Shooter Masterpieces You Need to Play
summary: From the original corridor shooter pioneers to the incredibly sophisticated genre hybrids of the 2020s, these are the 30 first-person shooter masterpieces you need to play.
content: Part of the promise of video games is putting yourself in another world, taking control of a character and experiencing adventure and excitement through their eyes. No genre takes this premise quite so literally as the first-person shooter, a pillar of the medium and a fundamental building block of the entire industry. There’s no shortage of shooters out there, but a select few stand above the rest as high-water marks for the art form. These are the 30 first-person shooter masterpieces you need to play The Pioneers Everything has to begin somewhere. For the first-person shooter, the primordial soup was a group of high school students working at a NASA study program in 1973. They created Maze War, a series of corridors you explored in hunt of another player to shoot. Unbeknownst to those students, they had triggered the start of an evolutionary chain that would lead to the creation of 100-player Warzone lobbies where victorious teenagers teabag the dead. But the first of something is rarely the best, nor the most influential. And so we look a little further ahead in the timeline to find the real pioneers. Wolfenstein 3D , id Software’s 1992 classic, is undoubtedly one of them. But that Nazi-plagued labyrinth was quickly overshadowed a year later by our first true masterpiece. Doom If the FPS has a main character, it’s the marine that sits in the middle of Doom ’s HUD. A representation of not just your unseen protagonist but also your health, his chiselled features are progressively marred by blood and bruises as you push on through some of the most focused firefights the genre has ever had to offer. Free from the burden of storytelling and lore, Doom is all about the kill. And there are so, so many kills. The garish corridors of Mars (and, later, Hell) are perfectly formed containers for exciting, kinetic, and challenging combat encounters. Back in 1993 we couldn’t even look up, but that didn’t stop id Software from assaulting us with an array of demons, both grounded and flying. Survival against such odds is made possible thanks to a small arsenal of weapons so purposeful in their design it makes modern shooters, with their army supply inventory, look like criminal waste – who needs (or even wants) 15 different SMGs when you can have the best shotgun in the business to gun down imps, and the chaingun with an RPM perfectly calibrated to interrupt a cacodemon’s fiery belches? Duke Nukem: 3D The early days of first-person shooters were an abstract affair, with blank-slate protagonists gliding through spartan research facilities and gothic labyrinths. The setting was more of a suggestion to keep you moving, bleary brick textures on ray-casted walls for your mute hero to grunt against in search of secret doors. Gamers were more than happy with the arrangement until a potty-mouthed, stogie-chomping, mildly misogynistic meathead showed them a better way. Apogee’s Duke Nukem 3D brought their EGA sidescrolling hero to a new dimension in the first hit shooter that dared to have a personality. Fully-voiced by Jon St. John, Duke oozed charisma, cracking jokes and one-liners appropriated from ‘80s action cinema. Fittingly, the first level sees Duke dropped onto an LA rooftop and fighting his way into an infested movie theater full of interactive objects, a far cry from the castles and space bases of his contemporaries. This was a first-person shooter that took place in our world, at our time, in places we could actually recognize, albeit with more burning barrels and floating powerups. The first-person POV was designed to help players embody their avatar, and Duke 3D was the first to make the world they inhabited just as immersive. Unreal Tournament 1999 is arguably the most important year in multiplayer history. Id Software continued to shape the bedrock of the entire FPS genre with Quake 3 Arena, an outstanding multiplayer hit whose engine would go on to power the behemoth that is Call of Duty. But just a few weeks earlier, Epic Games had shipped Unreal Tournament – the studio’s first dedicated PvP game, and the very first cog in the machine that would eventually become Fortnite. But even 27 years and hundreds of innovators later, Unreal Tournament remains perfectly formed. It is a library of phenomenal level design, with the industrial ramps and slime pools of DM-Deck16 providing the perfect arrangement of height and hazard for the ultimate deathmatch, and the symmetrical halves of the incredibly lean Facing Worlds providing the blueprint for every great Capture the Flag map. The arsenal is fantastic (particularly the ricocheting pellets ejected by the Flak Canon) and the action a gore-soaked adrenaline rush, but it’s the precision-engineered maps that make Unreal Tournament an immortal classic. Half-Life Valve does things differently. That’s a truth that goes right back to the developer’s very first game. Doom, Quake, and Unreal all have some kind of story wrapper, but they’re utilitarian – the gunplay is what drives them. Half-Life proved that narrative could be more than just a framework for FPS games. Gordon Freeman’s escape from a laboratory under siege is one of the richest stories a shooter has ever told, and it does it with barely any dialogue. Instead, the very walls and floors of the Black Mesa Research Facility provide the script – each new corridor and chamber the stage for a dramatic alien incursion or eerily quiet reveal. While Half-Life technically does have levels, the lab flows as one whole, continuous space, which cements it as a genuine place rather than a series of maps. The result is an experience that feels incredibly real, which only enhances the horror of your work colleagues being transformed into zombies. Doom (2016) Doom has remained a titan of shooters because it never ages. It’s constantly being reinvented and updated, typically by modding fans who have created some of the original game’s greatest levels. But id Software itself has also approached its hellish masterpiece in brand new ways, and the exceptional 2016 reboot of Doom is gaming’s best example of how to revitalise a franchise. The hyper-specific focus of the original game remains, but it’s elevated to impossible new heights by the punchiest gunplay you’ve ever pulled the trigger of. Your trusty shotgun rips demons apart, but when that’s not enough you can literally dig your hands in, tearing flesh to not just kill, but to replenish your own life force. This reboot arrived on the tail end of an era where shooters had been obsessed with cover and hunkering down to recover health. Doom said f*ck all that – to mend, you need to maul. And by tearing up the rule book, it restored the franchise’s HP to 100%. Console Champions So far, this could easily be mistaken for a list of the best PC games. When it comes to accuracy, the mouse is king, so of course many of the best shooters can be found on PC. But as soon as the analogue stick was invented, a whole new world was unlocked on consoles. While modern logic dictates that you need two sticks to make a shooter work, Nintendo has never been one for conventional thinking. The Nintendo 64 controller had just one analogue stick, and that carried us through one of the most seminal FPS games of all time… GoldenEye 007 Hailing from an era of Doom clones and developed by a team of novices at Rare, in hindsight it’s incredible that GoldenEye 007 became an iconic trailblazer. Rather than a straight up shooting gallery, its campaign acknowledged James Bond’s secret service employment through encouragement of stealth – there are no health packs here, and gunfire will summon curious guards, so tactical elimination of enemies is often the name of the game. Thankfully, an array of clever gadgets and then-novel tricks, like a sniper rifle with telescopic scope, offered methods of survival beyond just equipping the Klobb SMG for a bit of pray-and-spray. Of course, the Klobb’s ridiculous fire rate proved incredibly useful in GoldenEye’s unforgettable multiplayer. Featuring a collection of modes with objectives inspired by Bond’s adventures, such as You Only Live Twice’s two-lives-per-player, and The Man With The Golden Gun’s instakill 24-karat blaster, this was (and still is) the splitscreen champion of the world. Metroid Prime Nintendo may be best known as the home of the world’s greatest platformers, but GoldenEye proved you didn’t need a PC to play a groundbreaking FPS. A generation later, the big N continued to innovate: 2002’s Metroid Prime became the GameCube’s most essential shooter by stripping back the shooting. Yes, you are of course equipped with Samus Aran’s trademark arm cannon, and the surface of Tallon IV is home to plenty of enemies in need of blasting, but Metroid Prime takes a quieter approach to the FPS, prioritizing exploration over explosions. An effective translation of the series’ 2D values into a 3D world, puzzles and platforming are your core verbs here. Unlocking new equipment allows you to enter and survive new regions, and demolishing bosses arms you with an enjoyable selection of tools that ensures the galaxy’s coolest bounty hunter will take down her mark. Halo: Combat Evolved Bungie wanted to call its Xbox debut simply “Halo”. It was Microsoft that insisted on the “Combat Evolved” subtitle. As clunky and unnecessary as that addition is, though, it’s impossible to deny that it summarised the entire experience in two words. Back in 2001, Halo was an astonishing leap forward, and its advancements still have the capacity to enthrall a quarter century later. The campaign offers a perfectly balanced blend of tight corridor firefights and freeform, vehicle-friendly sandbox areas. Every single weapon not only feels punchy but fulfills a specific role, from the shield-splitting plasma rifle to the tank-busting SPNKr. Bungie’s star achievement, though, is its enemy AI, which turned the various ranks of the Covenant into a coherent fighting force, working together to flank, flush, and finish you. Responding realistically to incoming grenades and dwindling numbers, the Covenant breathes a genuine sense of life into Combat Evolved’s campaign. Of course, the multiplayer side of Halo didn’t need artificial intelligence – it had real players. While the explosive mix of Xbox Live and Halo 2 was yet to come, the original game’s splitscreen multiplayer remains a supreme example of how to upgrade classic deathmatch with refined maps, phenomenal weapons, and the wildcard addition of a swerving Warthog. Killzone 2 In the wake of Halo’s arrival, the race was on for PlayStation to find its own “Halo killer”. Several developers attempted, every one of them failed. But that’s not to say the hunt didn’t produce greatness. Guerrilla Games’ Killzone 2 is a master of hard, gritty sci-fi, its WW2-in-space aesthetic elevated to great heights thanks to once-mindblowing graphical quality that remains impressive to this day. All that lends the campaign a distinct atmosphere, but the real joy here is something that spans both single and multiplayer: really, really good guns. There are obvious favourites, like the skull-shattering M4 Revolver and the infantry-chewing StA-3 LMG, but every single one of Killzone 2’s weapons is lovingly crafted, with exceptional reload animations, fantastic audio design, and unique approaches that ensure every single one of them fulfills a distinct battlefield purpose. Destiny It wasn’t enough for Bungie to rewrite the FPS rulebook once. With Destiny , it took many of the ideas that fuelled Halo – unrivalled gunfeel, large environments, deep lore, and intense arena multiplayer – and spliced it with DNA from loot-driven games like Diablo and MMOs like World of Warcraft. The result was initially imperfect, with mission design that felt empty compared to the studio’s previous battlegrounds, as well as an over-reliance on grind. But as Destiny expanded, Bungie refined its online shooter formula, finding unique strength in raids – complex six-player co-op dungeons made up of a mix of fierce combat, cryptic puzzles, and tough boss encounters. By the time of Rise of Iron’s Wrath of the Machine and its spectacular Siege Engine, it was more than clear that Bungie had struck gold a second time. Big Thinkers Anyone who loves FPS games will reject the term “mindless shooter”, but there are plenty of gun games that certainly rely on reflexes more than mental aptitude. Serious Sam isn’t remotely concerned with your forward thinking or tactical planning. But, around the turn of the millenium, the genre saw a notable shift away from pure run-and-gun into more cerebral designs. These games thought outside the box – just what could a shooter played from first-person be? Deus Ex For developer Ion Storm, the answer was a cyberpunk conspiracy thriller where progression through the story had no rules. Deus Ex begins with a choice: will you arm yourself with a tranquiliser crossbow, a sniper rifle, or a rocket launcher? They’re more than just weapons – each option makes it clear that there are a multitude of ways to tackle the oncoming storm. Will you stealthily maneuver around the terrorists who have set up camp in New York City? Headshot them from afar? Or blow your enemies to smithereens? This guiding light asks you to consider the wider possibilities – if a door is locked, could you sneak in another way? Or can you simply blow it off its hinges? The answer to both is yes. And those solutions are arguably two of the most basic approaches on offer. Deus Ex is smart, and even 25 years later it’s easy to stumble across new possibilities on repeat playthroughs. The series had a brief modern resurgence with two brilliant prequel games – Human Revolution and Mankind Divided – although both are arguably less complex than their parent. But even if few have rivalled its malleability, Deus Ex opened the FPS up and gave it permission to think much, much bigger. BioShock The System Shock games of the late ‘90s whisked us away to abandoned space stations, where the story of their demise was gradually revealed through audio logs recorded by the long-dead. The series' successor, BioShock , adopted that framework while doubling down on the action. It loaded you up with not just an arsenal of guns, but also a collection of mutant abilities – including ice blasts that could freeze and fireballs that could melt – that proved the shock to the system that the FPS desperately needed in the late 2000s. Developer Irrational Games' most striking achievement, though, was creating a post-fall world that felt truly tragic. The underwater city of Rapture will forever be one of gaming’s best locations – its sprawling corridors and chambers hauntingly drawn in art deco brass and wood, populated by insane survivors, and given life by the fascinating ecosystem of gene-harvesting Little Sisters and their Big Daddy protectors. Combined with a story that smartly challenges not just Ayn Rand’s controversial politics, but also the assumptions of the player at the controls, BioShock is one of gaming’s unforgettable triumphs. SWAT 4 Irrational wasn’t just making philosophical statements in the 2000s, though – it also created one of history’s greatest tactical shooters. SWAT 4 puts you in command of a team of armed officers and deploys you into a series of crime scenes across New York City, where you’ll need to deal with objectives torn from the headlines. Bomb threats, hostage situations, nightclub shootings, and even hauling in a deranged serial killer are just some of the situations you’ll need to assess and contain. SWAT is dedicated to realism, so not only do you have to carefully order your team to scout rooms and issue orders in the correct sequence, but you also have to follow strict rules of engagement. Deaths are to be avoided at all cost, so non-lethal weapons are often your best option, and all suspects need to be arrested to achieve the optimum outcome. It all makes for an incredibly methodical shooter that rewards patience, planning, and perfect aim. Superhot There’s not much you can really do to innovate on the FPS formula. Different kinds of guns, unique levels, or interesting mechanics only go so far to dress up the core “pull trigger to make thing die” mode of interaction, and first-person brain-burners like Portal, while ingenious, don’t quite live up to the “shooter” side of the equation. Superhot is the exception, turning the core FPS verbs of movement and shooting into an intricate, mesmerizing puzzle. The 2016 indie sensation introduces a simple twist: time only moves when you do. Charging red enemies, rendered as stylized polygon humanoids, slow to a crawl while their bullets freeze in mid-air, letting you look around and plan your precious actions. You can shoot a pistol out of their hand, empty the magazine into your foe, fling the empty weapon at another and grab their shotgun before they can pull the trigger. SUPERHOT is a triumph of trial-and-error design made palatable by quick restarts and a huge possibility space. We haven’t seen anything like it since, save for SUPERHOT VR, which turns the clever experiment into a trippy, full-body experience that’s arguably the superior way to play. Half-Life: Alyx Valve’s dedication to authentic reality has guided Half-Life through a couple of industry-leading breakthroughs. Half-Life 2’s revolutionary physics introduced the laws of gravity in a way that has never truly been matched. But Valve’s most impressive reality has been virtual – Half-Life: Alyx is so ridiculously good that it alone (almost) justifies the cost of a VR headset. Transporting you onto the streets of City 17, this is a classic narrative FPS campaign completely recalibrated for virtual reality. Your own limbs’ physical reflexes can’t compare to the twitch controls of a mouse and keyboard, so Half-Life’s famously slippery firefights have been replaced with smaller scale battles. That may initially sound like a backstep, but the tension of being in a lethal shootout has never felt so real. Meanwhile, the zombie scares are dialed up to 11 (one of the best sequences asks you to literally cover your own mouth to mask your panicked breathing, lest an undead beast find you), and puzzles have been formatted to make full use of 3D space and tactile props. It all adds up to a world that you can really feel, and an adventure that’s more immediate than anything on a flat screen. It’s the best shooter the format has offered, but unfortunately few studios have the resources to follow in Valve’s footsteps. Beyond Corridors FPS games began as cramped affairs, trapped in mazes scrounging for keycards or pitted against opponents in bespoke arenas. The format is well-suited for ripping and tearing through demons or teabagging noobs in Midship, but one of the biggest benefits to a first-person perspective is immersion, the idea that we’re looking into an imaginary world through someone else’s eyes. It’s a format that invites exploration, and some of the genre’s greatest games make the most of a wide-open world. Metro Exodus The first two Metro games are deeply atmospheric linear shooters that inject the rough shape of Half-Life with an overdose of grim Eastern European horror. They’re good, but the series’ third entry, Metro Exodus , is a genuine all-timer. Released from Moscow’s underground tunnels and sent to find your destiny on the apocalyptic surface, you’re free to approach a chain of open hub worlds in any way you wish, be that striking from the shadows or unloading both barrels into anything that moves. A mix of smart human enemies and vicious mutants ensures all combat encounters keep you on your toes, and you’ll need to master a multitude of playstyles in order to effectively survive. If those expertly designed open environments were all Exodus had going for it, then it’d still be a fantastic FPS. But it’s elevated to masterpiece status by its story, which neatly interlocks with the game’s brutal combat mechanics to create one of the most effective horror experiences of the era. Cyberpunk 2077 The FPS doesn’t get much bigger than Cyberpunk 2077 . CD Projekt Red’s sci-fi masterpiece follows many of Deus Ex’s cues, including a vast array of body augmentations to unlock fascinating new playstyles, and level design that allows stealthy infiltrations, tactical hacking, and all-out gunfights. But unlike its leather-clad Y2K cousin, Cyberpunk 2077 is an epic-scale RPG set in a sprawling open world city. The narrative demands of that massive footprint means 2077 is second to none when it comes to worldbuilding – every street corner, market arcade, and towering megablock bleeds lore and environmental storytelling. As the rough-and-ready mercenary, V, you’ll take on seedy jobs featuring some of the genre’s most compelling storylines, from edge-of-your-seat espionage infiltrations to meditations on sin. In short, it has all the top-shelf quest design you’d expect from the developers of The Witcher, but you can make your enemies explode with guns that shoot homing bullets. It’s nothing short of preem. Far Cry 3 Ubisoft is one of the main culprits behind the modern open-world formula. Through Assassin’s Creed, the French developer popularized many of the genre’s most recognizable tropes, from climbing towers to reveal the landscape, enemy outposts scattered throughout progress-gated zones, and a minimap clogged with hundreds of icons. Far Cry 3 isn’t Ubisoft’s first attempt at an open world, but it’s the first time that the series took the lessons learned from its third-person contemporaries and applied them through a first-person lens. Coming off of the unfriendly, unforgiving, and still-unmatched intensity of Far Cry 2, the third game is where the series entered the triple-A canon. It applies the Assassin’s Creed framework to an uncharted island, with gorgeous tropical visuals placed front and center in your field of view. The gunplay and exploration are top-notch, but what distinguishes Far Cry 3 is its story and characters. Michael Mando’s star-making performance as the unhinged and volatile Vaas steals the show, while your own avatar Jason Brody grows from a clueless party bro captured by pirates into an apex predator with a magic skill tree tattoo, a wish-fulfilling power fantasy that only a first-person perspective can truly provide. Borderlands 2 You can’t have an FPS without guns. Lots of guns. Borderlands took this notion to the extreme, with a procedurally generated plethora of pew-pews that numbered in the tens of millions. Guns that dish out elemental damage, guns that explode when you throw them, guns with reverse recoil that get more accurate as you fire. It’s an entire language of guns, a lingua franca of firearms, and by the end you’ll be intimately familiar with the pros, cons, and quirks of the eight manufacturers who made them. Borderlands brought Diablo-style drops to first-person shooters and paved the way for future looter-shooters like The Division and Destiny, and it made such a splash in large part due to the overwhelming personality of its world. While the vibrant cel-shading and intense encounters still hold up, the character writing can seem cringe through our modern sensibilities, though that’s largely because of how influential the series became. Borderlands 2 , starring the unforgettable antagonist Handsome Jack, is the high point and easily stands on its own. Fallout: New Vegas Does New Vegas even count as a first-person shooter? It is first and foremost an RPG, after all, from one of the all-time great studios at the top of their game. The initial promise when Bethesda bought the franchise was “Oblivion with guns,” but Fallout 3 was less than stellar when it came to shooting. Obsidian improved on the foundation, introducing ironsights to make players less reliant on the methodical, turn-based-ish VATS system. Gunplay is further fleshed out by a bigger arsenal, weapon mods, and craftable specialty ammo, though the action on its own can’t really hang with most entries on this list. Where Fallout: New Vegas excels is, of course, in story and character. The betrayed Courier left for dead in the desert creates a customized journey in every playthrough, navigating the complex factions that call the Mojave Wasteland home and living with the consequences of their choices. Endearing companions and fascinating antagonists give our quests meaning, while the aesthetic and lore of Fallout have never shone brighter than under the sun-bleached Nevada sky. Lots of other shooters have embraced RPG storytelling, but there’s never been another New Vegas. Multiplayer Monarchs First-person shooters have never been a solo affair. The most primordial iterations on massive mainframes pit players against each other, and as the genre grew so did the thirst for competition. Simple games of hide and seek became thrilling tests of skill and reflex while LAN parties paved the way for Xbox Live and our modern online infrastructure. Multiplayer is the FPS in its purest form, and if you disagree, we’d be happy to 1v1 you over it. Overwatch The notion of Blizzard, the developers behind top-down, zoomed-out strategy games and online RPGs, crafting a competitive, high-octane first-person shooter seemed dubious at first. Overwatch , however, triumphed by doing what Blizzard does best: borrowing from everyone else. The same way they lifted hulking green orcs and armored blue space marines from Warhammer, Blizzard took the class system and objective-first design from Team Fortress 2, fused it with the cooldown management and counterpicking of MOBAs, and slathered the whole package in a glossy layer of Pixar charm. In a genre like FPS that tends to skew more hardcore, Overwatch was truly for everyone. You could casually enjoy the charming characters in Quick Play, scrape against your Platinum plateau in Ranked, or chase the esports dream in a huge pro scene that arose almost overnight. Like any live service game, Overwatch has changed drastically over the course of its existence, and most veterans can point out the moment where they felt it left them behind: nerfing Mercy’s ult, Brigitte and the infamous GOATS meta, role lock, the cancelled PvE experience and the strange saga of Overwatch 2. These evolutionary shifts are common and even necessary for a long-running multiplayer title to survive, and the game is still going strong today as a result, but that first year or so was pure magic, cementing Overwatch as a modern masterpiece. Quake 3 Arena Who cares about Quake campaigns? Not John Carmack, the id Software co-founder who famously likened video game plots to those of pornography in terms of importance. Like its contemporary Unreal Tournament, 1999’s Quake 3 Arena eschews any real single-player content in exchange for bot-based skirmishes that simulate the game’s true draw: a high-octane contest of skill and strategy that demands total command of aim, movement, and map knowledge. Quake 3 is spartan by modern standards. There’s no aiming down the sights here– you won’t have time, since the second you stop moving at ludicrous speed you’ll be fragged out of existence by a railgun blast. You won’t find upgrade systems and character progression to boost your K/D here. In Quake 3 the only improvement is self-improvement. The only way to win is to learn the maps, control the items, and above all else, hit your shots. Quake 3 Arena and the community that coalesced around it helped carry competitive gaming into the new millennium with a bevy of fan-made mods and modes that built on the base game’s purity of pwnage. Battlefield: Bad Company 2 Many of the multiplayer shooters on this list are surprisingly small in scale, where you battle alone or with a handful of teammates across a fairly limited map. EA and DICE’s Battlefield series blows all that up in spectacular fashion, with vast conflicts involving dozens of combatants spanning destructible environments that require an entire fleet of vehicles to navigate. It’s all out war in FPS form, and you’re in the driver’s seat. The series has seen its share of swings and misses through the decades, but in aggregate the highs outweigh the lows. From the original Battlefield 1942, to the HD reinvention of Battlefield 3, and the bold left turn of Battlefield 1, DICE has usually met the industry moment and offered a viable, sometimes superior alternative to Call of Duty’s dominance. When it comes to masterpieces, one game in the series stands out as a complete package: Battlefield: Bad Company 2 . The game’s punky, irreverent attitude, loveable squad of ragtag misfits, and a solid single-player campaign are the icing on top of a masterfully crafted and balanced multiplayer experience. You’d do well with nearly any Battlefield, but Bad Company 2 brings the most joy. ARMA 3 In the military, there’s a concept called “the suck,” a catch-all term for the mind-numbing mundanity, back-breaking labor, danger and suffering that defines the days of those who serve. Arma is a video game series that embraces the suck, that attempts to capture the miserable conditions of combat from the comfort of your computer. Games like CoD and Battlefield do everything they can to avoid the suck. They’re all about empowerment, getting you in the action as fast as possible with the tools and abilities you need to cap objectives and rack up kills. Arma asks a lot more of you. You fine-tune every decision of the tactical simulation as you fight and die across an island spanning hundreds of square kilometers. You reckon with exhaustion and fatigue and the weight of your loadout while eyeballing bullet drops in the accurately modeled ballistics amid an unforgiving damage model that will end you in an instant. Arma’s legacy goes beyond just “really hard shooters,” however. DayZ began as an Arma 2 mod that inspired a vast army of open-world survival sims. The DayZ mod, in turn, was transformed into PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds, sparking the Battle Royale revolution that begat Fortnite, Warzone, Apex Legends, and countless others. For a game that’s so unfriendly to play, its generosity to modders allowed Arma to birth something far bigger. Left 4 Dead 2 Can’t we all just get along? The multiplayer conversation around FPS is predominantly centered on competition, but there’s plenty of fun to be had in fighting with, not against, your friends to fend off an escalating horde of enemies. Co-operative shooters can offer some of the most intense experiences in all of gaming, and they don’t get much better than Left 4 Dead 2 . Valve didn’t waste any time cranking out a sequel to its 2008 hit Left 4 Dead, which thrust players into the role of four survivors bursting with personality as they struggled through a zombie apocalypse in campaigns presented like a grindhouse cinema matinee. Valve drew sharp criticism for moving on from the slightly flawed original after only a year, as Left 4 Dead 2 made the first game more or less obsolete. What’s fascinating about Left 4 Dead 2 is that there’s really nothing like it anymore. No one has pushed the AI “Director,” which analyzed how players were doing and adjusted the experience mid-game for maximum tension, much further. The asymmetry of L4D2’s versus mode, where opposing players control superpowered special infected, found its heirs in modern horror games like Dead by Daylight and Halloween, which pit only one beefed-up monster against a squad of victims. Horde modes have similarly fallen out of favor for bigger co-op sandboxes, with the closest cousin probably being Helldivers 2. Coming at the start of the pop-culture zombie boom and the height of Valve’s beast-mode Orange Box era, we may never see a co-op shooter with this much sauce again. The Top 5 Twenty-five masterpieces isn’t too shabby for a genre that can be reduced to “click things to make them die,” and we still aren’t finished. The following five first-person shooters represent the absolute best the format has to offer, the true titans of their field. Speaking of which… Titanfall 2 Many a masterpiece is built from the bones of something that showed a lot of promise but didn’t quite work– Picasso famously painted several of his Blue Period classics on top of earlier portraits and landscapes he’d abandoned. Titanfall, from CoD masterminds Jason West and the late Vince Zampella, was similarly half-formed when the series debuted. It delivered on the dev’s trademark twitch action with a wall-running, sci-fi twist, while the MOBA-style action involved farming NPC grunts to summon your Titan, a hulking yet surprisingly nimble machine that let you dominate the battlefield. It was an intriguing gimmick that controlled beautifully, switching from boots-on-the-ground infantry combat to towering mech battles in an instant, but the game felt incomplete without a meaningful single-player component. Respawn addressed the lack of campaign in the first Titanfall by creating one of the all-time greats in Titanfall 2 . You are Jack Cooper, rifleman in the Frontier Militia, who finds himself piloting a Titan bequeathed to him by his dying mentor. Over the course of the breezy, perfectly-paced story, Cooper and BT-7274 form an irreplaceable buddy cop bond. Through bloodshed and banter we and Cooper come to love the big lunk, caring deeply for this literally faceless machine. The campaign is split across nine missions built around “action blocks,” scenarios that each showcase a single idea. Into the Abyss sends you on a desperate search for your best pal BT through an assembly-line gauntlet in an underground factory, while the Ark is an aerial chase through the skies of Typhon. The most celebrated mission, Effect and Cause, introduces time travel into the mix, allowing you to swap between a ruined building and its pristine past in an extremely clever triumph of design that could easily carry its own game. Titanfall 2 failed to meet sales expectations, but again, not every masterpiece is defined by financial success. Just ask Van Gogh. What makes a masterpiece is the way they move us, how we remember them through the years, and the countless other artists they inspire. Doom Eternal Doom is the blueprint for the modern FPS, so there are a lot of expectations for a Doom game that dares to reinvent it. Doom 2016 was more of an upgrade, bringing the old feel up to speed for a new generation. Doom Eternal pushes beyond the bounds of boomer shooters into something completely different. In Doom 2016, the super shotgun can carry the Slayer through most encounters without breaking a sweat, but the economy of Eternal demands more variety. Resources are scarce, making glory kills a must, finishing off your foes in particular ways to replenish yourself. Ammo is harder to come by, and so is the chainsaw fuel that makes it magically erupt from demonic viscera. Sturdier demons require specific weapons and tactics to take down. All of it forces you to rely on more of your arsenal to survive every hellish encounter, working nearly every button on the controller with attacks, belches, and things that go boom. FPS is traditionally the realm of Western developers, a genre born in Texas and still dominated by American and European studios. Doom Eternal is the first to feel like a Japanese character action game, Devil May Cry from behind Doomguy’s visor, double dashing through demon-infested skies raining bullets on the swarms above and below. It rewards skill and acrobatics and demands mastery of your inputs if you dream of surviving the Super Gore Nest. It’s a marvel that you’re not awarded S-ranks for stylish slaying. Some prefer the stripped-down simplicity of Doom 2016, particularly its lighter touch on lore, but Doom Eternal is unlike any other FPS on the market, a gamer’s game that must be experienced to truly comprehend its carnage. Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare Everyone plays Call of Duty. Your cousin plays Call of Duty. The guys on Love Island play Call of Duty. If the algorithm brought you here, statistically speaking you probably play Call of Duty. First-person shooters are the main and often only way some people interact with video games at all, and it’s all thanks to Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare . The franchise was still in a healthy spot in 2007, though the World War 2 setting was becoming rote after years of industry exploitation. Gamers were ready to move on from the six-year period that defined the 20th century for something that reflected the less morally sound conflicts of the world outside their window. Modern Warfare was exactly what FPS needed. Infinity Ward delivered a globetrotting, blockbuster war story with Tom Clancy verisimilitude and a summer movie scale. Combat is big and bombastic, with regenerating health and endless swarms of enemy soldiers for us to ADS out of existence. More importantly, CoD 4’s multiplayer unleashed an addictive rush of unlockables, customization, and killstreaks. It was an experience that would one day become worth drinking Mountain Dew for, if only for the double XP, but the original Modern Warfare best represents the balance of design and dopamine that cemented the first-person shooter as the public face of gaming. Counter-Strike 2 Counter-Strike is a video game in the same sense that chess is a board game: technically true, but it has ascended so far beyond the category it belongs to that it exists in a space all its own. And just like the rules of chess have been static for centuries, changing anything fundamental about CS is tantamount to sacrilege, like adding free throws to baseball. We’re specifically including Counter-Strike 2 because that’s just how those fundamentals are currently packaged, but it’s not all that different from the mod that came out last millennium. Counter-Strike simply is , and no one can touch it. Two teams of five players must either plant a bomb or defuse it. Each round opens with a buying phase, where your performance dictates what you can afford to bring into battle. Winning requires knowing where to place your crosshair to catch an opponent as they turn a corner, which angles to hold, and even which rounds to sacrifice on purpose. It’s the kind of game you practice for, with aim trainers and minutely dialed-in DPI settings on your mouse. Counter-Strike isn’t something you really approach casually, yet it’s the most-played game on all of Steam, regularly peaking at well over a million players on any given day. Counter-Strike has no campaign to speak of, but there’s an incredible story behind the game itself. It began as a free mod for Half-Life in 1999, before Valve quickly snapped up the property and hired its creators. CS is the ultimate realization of the PC FPS scene’s DIY spirit, a game made by gamers as a gift to other gamers, and everything is downstream from there. The legendary de_dust map was made by a bedroom coder, as were Gun Game and the mod that would become Prop Hunt, both hugely influential in the wider FPS space. No matter how slick the tournaments get or how big the prize pools grow, there remains a refreshing lack of corporate gloss to Counter-Strike. It’s the FPS that belongs to everyone. Half-Life 2 Half-Life 2 ’s unforgettable onboarding experience begins in City 17, with Gordon Freeman picking up a can under the grating gaze of Dr. Breen. Every new chapter unlocks a new facet of the gameplay experience, from blasting through canals on an airboat to find the gravity gun at Black Mesa East and putting it to the test in the boobytrapped town of Ravenholm. Half-Life 2’s Havok physics sent shockwaves through the industry, basically mandating the presence of seesaw puzzles and collapsible scaffolds for years to come. Half-Life 2 achieves something special in its embodiment of Gordon Freeman. It’s rare to vanish so completely into an avatar, but we find ourselves subsumed by the geeky MIT grad who once had a ponytail. The game’s stakes and drama don't come through cutscenes, they’re around us all the time as expertly staged scenes large and small. It’s the purest form of first-person storytelling that’s rarely been equaled. Half-Life 2 is unbelievable. It’s impossible for a character created from 8,000 polygons to make us feel something without facial-captured pathos from scanned-in A-list actors. It’s inconceivable that a game forced to launch through a loathed new DRM scheme could turn it into the industry’s most dominant platform. It’s unthinkable that a game made before the age of ironsights and regenerating health could stand as a timeless pinnacle for what an FPS can achieve. If you could only play one first-person shooter in your lifetime, Half-Life 2 would show you exactly what they stand for. Thanks for reading, everyone. Did any of your favorites not make the list? What do you think makes an FPS masterpiece? Should we have included Portal? Leave a comment, let us know, and stay tuned to IGN for more first-person fragging fun.

title: Someone Is Making One of Baldur's Gate 3's Most Popular Villains Romanceable
summary: One of Baldur's Gate 3's main villains, Gortash, could be romanceable soon thanks to this new fan-made mod.
content: Baldur's Gate 3 has no shortage of romances and romantic encounters, but not everyone in Faerûn is up for a smooch. When developer Larian was still rolling out updates, fans would often ask for more romances to be added, whether it be for Jaheira or Rolan, but it was never meant to be. One of the most popular requests was actually for one of Baldur's Gate 3's main villains, Gortash. Larian was very much aware of this, and actually addressed these fans in the patch notes in 2024. "Listen, he’s a complicated guy who’s busy contemplating the minutia of death cult office politics," Larian said at the time. "Babygurl doesn’t have time to kiss." But now, a fan is stepping up, adding the Gortash romance that so many were asking for. TikTok user Equipouet has shared some clips from the mod, which is still a work in progress. It shows the player character being invited to spend time with Gortash, played by Lucius Malfoy actor Jason Isaacs, after his coronation in Act 3, all with new dialogue and animations. We're told that we'll be able to make our own choices when we meet Gortash, specifically whether we want to "charm him, keep him guessing, or walk away." So, if you really hate Gortash, you could also use the mod to let him down. Much more is teased for the mod, like a ball held by Gortash, letters to exchange with him, and "choices with consequences." There will also be changes to how the story plays out if your character is The Dark Urge, since it's in your backstory that you already have a history with Gortash. The mod is still being worked on, but the author says they will submit it for console release approval once it's done. That process can be lengthy, however, and there's no guarantee that it will pass the approval stage, especially if it's too bulky for console. In the meantime, Gortash kissers will keep having to use their imagination. Like us would-be Jaheira kissers. There are also plenty of other mods to try out, including a bunch that have Larian's seal of approval and can be installed within the game's own mod manager. Image credit: Larian.

title: BioWare Fans Hit Out at EA for Selling New Dragon Age Merch After Killing the Studio
summary: A new Dragon Age hoodie is available on the BioWare Gear store, as EA continues to sell merch based on BioWare's now dead franchises.
content: EA's decision to shut down BioWare sparked a mix of shock and sadness across the internet , with both fans and developers fondly remembering the many role-playing games the Canadian studio put out over the years. The Mass Effect community has been especially vocal , given that Mass Effect 5 was cancelled alongside the studio closure . But Dragon Age fans certainly aren't happy either, and they're making it known. Despite BioWare's closure, the BioWare Gear merch store is still being updated. A bunch of new items were added for N7 Day , but we just got a new Dragon Age merch drop too. For example, the Dragon Age Inquisition Seven of Swords Nightmare Hoodie features a piece of tarot card art that appears in Dragon Age: Inquisition. Better still, the art depicts fan-favourite character Duncan from Dragon Age: Origins. But given that we're only getting this hoodie after everyone who worked on the Dragon Age series lost their job, it isn't sitting well with fans. "Do not give #EA the privilege of royalties on IP they have killed, and will not sell or forfeit," one fan said . "If you want your voice heard and want to #SaveDragonAge and #SaveMassEffect, EA needs to reckon with the consequences of their bad financial decisions. #BoycottEA and licensed merch." "Save Mass Effect. Save Dragon Age. Dragon Age was failed massively by EA. You destroyed what Veilguard could have/should have been because you pushed for it to be live service then backtracked. You never gave Dragon Age the chance it deserved," another person replied to the BioWare Gear Store's post promoting the hoodie . "No studio, No Game = No money," Olarcadia said on X / Twitter . "What you're doing is a pure lack of respect." "It's so cute how you think putting out merch is going to make us hate you any less," onedcdame agreed. "Keep it. BioWare is closed, we're not giving you any of our money EA," replied SignWithBlood. "You should offer to sell back the IP to the founders, including the BioWare brand and name," added @inkpot__gods. "We bought merch to support the devs who made the games we loved; you fired all the devs and stopped making those games, so there’s no one left for us to financially support," said LouEaglesham. It appears that the community plans to boycott EA's continued use of BioWare's IPs, at least until it allows a team of devs to make a new game in these universes. Right now, both Dragon Age and Mass Effect are on ice. Dragon Age fans in particular have a lot to be upset about. The last game in the series, Dragon Age: The Veilguard, largely failed to impress the community. But it has long been known that the game languished in development hell and suffered from various changes in direction. Former BioWare executive producer Mark Darrah recently shared the original vision for the fourth Dragon Age game , before EA allegedly mandated that it had to be a live service. EA would then go on to allow the game to be retooled as a single-player RPG, but The Veilguard had to be built from the bones of this live service work, meaning the developers didn't have time to return to this original outline. It remains to be seen what EA does next with the Dragon Age series. EA is not in the habit of selling off IP, but if enough fans are boycotting the merch, it leaves EA without much to do other than just sit on it.

title: Despite Take-Two Takedown, Vibecoding Teen Behind Nuked GTA 6 PC Port Project 'Leonida' Vows to Continue
summary: The 15-year-old vibecoder behind a GTA 6 PC port project Take-Two recently shut down has vowed to continue their work despite the potential for further action from the company.
content: The 15-year-old vibecoder behind a GTA 6 PC port project Take-Two recently shut down has vowed to continue their work despite the potential for further action from the company. ‘NotRexed’ is behind ‘Project Leonida,’ which was at one point leading the race to create a PC port of GTA 6 following the recent leak of an Xbox build. Cyberleek, the infamous leaker behind many early GTA 6 gameplay clips, reportedly released the Xbox build of GTA 6 last week, and vibecoders have been attempting to port the game to PC since. Fueled by AI, progress has been swift, with clips showing GTA 6 running on PC at a higher frame rate than on console, and one video even showing basic multiplayer. Obviously, Rockstar Games, which will no doubt release GTA 6 on PC officially at some point, and parent company Take-Two will be watching the homebrew scene’s every move like a hawk. In the case of Project Leonida, Take-Two has already taken action. NotRexed was organizing and sharing work on a Discord group, and hosting their findings on a GitHub repository, when cease and desists from Take-Two hauled everything offline. NotRexed then took to social media to announce they'd decided to call it a day. “I quit guys. I’m sorry,” NotRexed said. “I really want to make cool stuff but every single time s**t happens that I can’t control so I’m stepping away. Thank you everybody, especially in the Discord that allowed me to have this opportunity.” NotRexed went on to insist that they were finding it tough to run Project Leonida while also going to school. “Rockstar taking my server down was only part of the reason. Like I’ve said before, I’m a 15-year-old kid,” they said. “Managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on Discord. Goodbye.” However, NotRexed has now returned, and promised to continue the project. “Ignore my other posts,” NotRexed said after changing their mind. “Something’s coming soon. Leonida is NOT dead. I have been doing a lot of work behind the scenes. I’ll have some stuff to show all of you soon.” IGN spoke to NotRexed to find out why they’re doing this, whether they understand the risks, what they’ll do if they get in legal trouble, and what their parents think of it all. “It’s just a hobby of mine,” NotRexed said in a private message. “I started doing similar things with porting games to the web back in the start of 2026, and I’ve always just thought of it to be cool.” Before generative AI, NotRexed had no interest in porting games to other platforms, they said. But after finding out it was possible in 2025, they’re now taking on one of the most powerful publishers in video games. Interestingly, there’s no real motive behind it. “I’ve always been interested in tech and mess around with it a lot,” they said. According to them, even their parents are aware of what they do and are largely supportive of it. “Yes, they know about all my projects and work I do, and they’re pretty encouraging about it,” they claimed. It made me wonder if they were fully aware of the legal risks involved in such an undertaking. “Yea, they have warned me about what could happen,” NotRexed insisted when I asked if their parents knew about the potential legal issues. “I’m still continuing my work as of now tho because even tho T2 took down my repo and Discord they have never sent an email or message directly to me. If I do get into legal trouble I’m probably gonna stop working on it but possibly have a friend continue it.” How feasible is this? IGN asked Matt Freedman, a veteran game developer with expertise in both traditional development and the controversial emerging technology of AI. “A recompilation is different from a port,” Freedman said. “But yes, an AI driven recompilation of GTA 6 is very doable and wouldn't have the same 'game feel' problems that an AI-driven port would have.” He went on to explain the differences between decompilations, recompilations, and ports. A decomp is where someone manually reverse engineers a game to run on other systems, like the Mario 64 PC port. “This is very time consuming and requires a human to do the work and effectively 'guess' how the game works,” he said. A port takes existing assets or creates new ones and essentially builds a new version of the same game to work on another system. The Witcher 3’s Switch port is an example of this. “A team took The Witcher 3 code base and assets and then modified them by hand to work on the Switch,” he said. For recomps, people use large language models (LLMs) to break down a game and rebuild it, essentially reverse engineering the title for whatever system the user wants. “Since LLMs natively can read binary, they're able to understand the specific code better than humans can,” Freedman explained. A decomp or port of GTA 6 would not be easy — not least because Rockstar uses proprietary tech, including its in-house Rage engine, to power its games. “When it comes to AI, it'll depend on how well it has previously seen the engine or the low level SDK,” Freedman replied when asked about this complication. “A well studied proprietary engine with lots of public information would be easier for it to understand. A custom engine for an obscure CPU would be much more difficult for it. “So, something like Rockstar's Rage engine would be more difficult for it to figure out than something like a game made in Unreal. But… given that a 15-year-old was able to have an AI port GTA 6 to PC, it's clearly not the biggest lift out there.” All the while, Take-Two is working to take down various homebrew community efforts from GitHub, as the race to release an unofficial GTA 6 PC port appears close to the finish line. There’s even a website tracking the various attempts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox Series build to PC. The big question for Take-Two is, can it do anything meaningful to stop a working, playable build of GTA 6 on PC from getting into people's hands? GitHub takedowns can only go so far, as the homebrew scene uses AI to speed along development. It's a question IGN recently asked when people started to work on a PC port of Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake . Take-Two stands to make billions of dollars more from the official PC release of GTA 6, so any unofficial version is a significant business risk. In a recent interview with IGN sister site RPS , former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij said that Rockstar may be keen to port GTA 6 to PC as soon as possible , due to the explosion of AI-generated clones and ports. Earlier this month, Strauss Zelnick, the boss of Take-Two, responded to the threat of AI-assisted reverse-engineering and decompilation of games in an interview with IGN. He said he was taking the issue seriously, and insisted that fans will prefer to play GTA 6 officially, as Rockstar intended, over an unofficial PC version. Here’s the exchange: IGN: We've seen hackers using AI to clone games much faster than ever before, even try to jailbreak consoles. And there is some concern about this leading to potentially GTA 6 being made available on PC unofficially or places that you aren't releasing it. I was just wondering how much of a threat this is to your business? And, is there anything meaningful you can do about it? Strauss Zelnick: I don't think it’s a financial matter, in terms of a threat to our business. I do think it’s a creative matter. It's important to everyone, our developers and our consumers alike, to deliver the experience Rockstar envisions. And at the same time, of course, we protect our intellectual property vigilantly. So we are focused on these concerns. We're not in the least cavalier about them. Technology is advancing quickly. And at the same time, I do think that pretty much everyone wants the Rockstar experience as Rockstar intended. IGN: Related, last week Anthropic confirmed they took steps to block Claude from reverse engineering video games. I would assume you would welcome that. And would you like to see other AI companies like OpenAI do the same thing to prevent people from using these powerful AI models to clone your games? Strauss Zelnick: I think all companies should be protecting intellectual property, their own and everyone else's. And if you're in the intellectual property business, which Anthropic is and OpenAI is, then it seems ironic on the one hand to stomp on someone else's IP and hope that yours is protected. During an investor-focused Q&A following the release of Take-Two’s latest financial report, attended by IGN, Zelnick was asked multiple times about the AI reverse-engineering problem. He, again, had strong words in response, suggesting Take-Two was ready to lawyer up. “This business has been largely immune to piracy concerns forever because of file sizes, complexity of piracy, being connected to servers and the like,” he began. “And undoubtedly, it would be very difficult to replicate the experience of consuming our game as intended because of technical limitations. “That said, it's going to become more of a challenge, as you said, and we're aware of that. So we are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And at the same time, without in any way being cavalier, every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy. So this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it.”

title: Former Gran Turismo World Series Competitor Helped Tune GTA 6 Car Physics
summary: A former Gran Turismo World Series competitor helped Rockstar tune GTA 6's car physics.
content: A lot of people have complained about the Ganado, Jason’s starting car in GTA 6 , for being tricky to drive. The small pickup is a little unwieldy and prone to swinging out at the back end because it’s based on the Ford Ranchero, a rear-wheel drive whip manufactured between 1957–1979 in North America. While there are no licensed vehicles in GTA 6, cars are recognisable based on real-world counterparts, with small visual changes to make them legally distinct. But the accuracy doesn’t stop at the car model — it also extends to how they drive. That variety in handling is in part because Rockstar hired Lewis Bentley, a former Gran Turismo World Series competitor, to work on the vehicle physics team. Bentley announced the news in a now-deleted YouTube video. “We put the auto in the Grand Theft Auto,” he said from the driver’s seat of his Lotus Elise. Bentley is best known for qualifying for the final in the GT Sport World Tour event at the Nürburgring 24 Hours, in 2018. “Everyone on the physics team’s amazing,” he said in the same video. He claimed to have worked on GTA 6 for around three years in total, and is listed in the game’s credits as a developer in the physics department. Bentley isn’t the only gearhead who worked on the game, however. Rockstar North has its own in-house racing team , and they’re pretty good on the track — they won a team-based 24h Nürburgring event back in 2022. You can see this attention to detail in the game, both in vehicle handling models on cars and on the tracks. For the first time in the series, GTA 6 features a closed asphalt circuit called Gellhorn International Raceway, which stitches together a bunch of iconic corners and racing lines from some of the most famous real-world tracks in existence, turning them into the ultimate speedway. We’ve got the Official Grand Theft Auto 6 guide here on IGN, complete with comprehensive walkthroughs up to Chapter 5 , guides for the Optional Missions and Illegal Operations you’ll find in Leonida, and much more. title: Hollow Knight: Silksong - Sea of Sorrow Launch Trailer Finally Confirms Release Date, Teases Fishing
summary: Team Cherry's latest showcase gives us a release date for Sea of Sorrow, the free DLC expansion coming to Hollow Knight: Silksong, and a launch trailer.
content: Team Cherry has just wrapped up its Cherry Time! showcase, giving us some long-awaited news on the future of Hollow Knight: Silksong. The big takeaway here is that Hollow Knight: Silksong's first big expansion, Sea of Sorrow, finally has a release date of December 11. Sea of Sorrow will be available to all Silksong players for free. All you need is a copy of the base game, and you can start playing Sea of Sorrow when it goes live on December 11. This also means Team Cherry has stuck to its promise to get Sea of Sorrow out by the end of the year. Some had feared that today's announcement would be a delay — or an announcement that the DLC was being expanded into a full game, which is famously how Silksong's development began. In the showcase, we got a new look at Sea of Sorrow's gameplay. This gives us a good preview of what's in store for us, as we see new areas, enemies, and boss fights. Of course, it all looks as challenging as ever, as you'd expect for Silksong's post-launch DLC. And is that a fishing mini-game teased at the end? We weren't told anything else about the future of Silksong or the Hollow Knight series at large. There was no mention of this being Silksong's only expansion, so it's very possible that Team Cherry plans to support the game beyond Sea of Sorrow. For now, here's the official blurb on Sea of Sorrow: In Sea of Sorrow, players will voyage above and beneath Pharloom’s forgotten ocean, across islands, through forts and into deep caverns beneath the waves. We’ve spent the whole year stuffing this adventure full with all the things you’d expect from Hollow Knight: Silksong - crazed characters, high adventure, and epic bosses! It’s also overflowing with more exceptional music by the eternally talented Christopher Larkin! We’re pretty darn excited to get it into all of your hands on December 11, so please look forward to it. Outside of this reveal, Team Cherry used the attention to promote indie games from other studios. Three were shown off: Blokkan: Secret of the Walking City, which is fully hand-drawn; Radio Rain, which is centred around 1980s-inspired music; and The Botanist and the Translator, which boasts a Sailor Moon-esque vibe. In a follow-up blog post , Team Cherry confirmed that these new games will release under the new Team Cherry Presents label, which is headed up by the indie developer's fourth team member, Huy Le. Huy is technical director and on-going support for all the Team Cherry Presents games, but has also helped out on Silksong and Sea of Sorrow. "As a long-time team of three people, adding a fourth member is a big deal!" Team Cherry said.

title: I Tried to Get Six Stars in GTA 6 With Just One Bullet and Broke the Game
summary: We tried to get six stars in GTA 6 by firing just one bullet and broke the game.
content: If reaching a six-star wanted level in Grand Theft Auto 6 is your goal, there are many different methods available to you. Raiding the military base for a tank is one way. Committing a horrifying beach massacre is another. But can you get there by firing just a single bullet? We at IGN had a theory that this was absolutely possible, and so spent hours in a fast food joint to find out. When we say “by firing a single bullet,” we mean that technically speaking. Our theory is that your chosen character only needs to pull the trigger once. That’s because, when roaming around GTA 6’s open world and causing whatever brand of chaos you’ve chosen to, your partner will automatically take up the fight against aggressors, and is both invulnerable and stocked with unlimited ammunition. That means if you decide to walk into a heavily populated area as a couple and fire just one bullet into the crowd, your better half can commit the lion's share of the atrocities themselves, provided you just stay alive. We tested this out for ourselves, leading Jason and Lucia to the Taco Bomb in Gellhorn as our chosen arena of violence. Taking control of Jason, one bullet was fired into a poor staff member taking a break outside. Bits of brain now covered the forecourt, which somehow still looked like a more appetising alternative to whatever the questionable-looking beef was they were offering inside. Creeping cannibalistic thoughts pushed to one side, we walked back inside knowing our work was done. This public execution, perhaps rightfully, attracted a police patrol car to the restaurant, of which Lucia did not take kindly to their arrival. Her love for Jason knows no bounds, up to and including unloading full machine gun magazines into any cops who want to arrest him. And who were we to stand in her way? Letting her take control of the situation was then required, honorably moving Jason behind the indestructible cover of an industrial refrigerator. Sporting an armoured vest just in case any stray bullets or shrapnel found their way around the corner, it was then time to hunker down in the kitchen beside that thick metal fridge, out of view of law enforcement. Crucially, this fast food establishment’s kitchen does not have a door leading outside, meaning the threat of flanking cops was neutralised. Luckily, they didn’t seem to spot the drive-thru window, which would’ve handed them a clean shot. Could a six-star wanted level be achieved by us, the player, firing just one bullet? And there we sat for a good 45 minutes as Lucia angrily gunned down anyone brave enough to step into the restaurant. No more food would be served today, only death. The red of discarded hot sauce packets replaced by the blood of the fallen. The crunch of hard shell tacos drowned out by the crack of broken bones. All in the name of science. Could a six-star wanted level be achieved by us, the player, firing just one bullet? Well, not this time. We could’ve sat here forever, bravely hiding behind a fridge while our partner slaughtered hundreds. Lucia was invincible, rounds of ammunition sinking into her skin to no effect. She had no shortage of ammo herself; with an unlimited pool of lead to reload from, she could’ve done this all day, and all for us. If that isn’t true romance, I don’t know what is. Day turned to night, and the restaurant workers diligently remained kneeling behind the counter and cowering for the whole sordid ordeal. The problem is, our aggressors just… stopped. After a period of quiet, we chose to break cover and wander outside, only to be met by several non-aggravated members of law enforcement staring blankly at us. We had seemingly confused them with our methods of madness. Because we’re so dedicated to the cause here at IGN, we tried all over again. Putting this first attempt down as an unfortunate glitch, we reloaded a save, made our way to Taco Bomb, and fired a single gunshot into our chosen test subject. And so, another hour of hiding behind a fridge commenced while our incredibly committed girlfriend peppered anyone who dared approach us with bullets. Armoured trucks eventually surrounded the exits, and the sound of helicopter blades could be heard above. But the same thing happened again. We even waited long enough for the rest mode settings on our PS5 to almost put the console to sleep. Could just one grenade be our key to maxing out the wanted level? It seems GTA 6 gets very confused if you decide to start a chain reaction like this, only to go passive for the next 60 minutes. Again, five stars were secured on the wanted level, but that sixth just wouldn’t arrive. The enemy AI’s brain could not comprehend what was happening, so we decided we simply had to intervene. If that sixth star was going to be ours, we’d need to get involved ourselves. Thus, we thought we’d honor the place we’d called home for the past couple of hours, and end our occupancy of Taco Bomb with an explosion. A bunch of incapacitated, but not dead, cops lay writhing on the floor of the restaurant. Could just one grenade be our key to maxing out the wanted level? There was only one way of finding out. We ended the whole bloody affair with a bang, ripping the pin out of the explosive before hurling it into the mound of bodies. And that’s when it happened. Nirvana. The gates of heaven opened. Six-star paradise was ours to bask in. So, what was the point of all of this? Well, more than anything, to confirm that you never have to worry about Jason or Lucia dying when roaming around GTA 6’s open world when not controlling them. Unlike in missions, where they can slip off this mortal coil, they can’t die in free-roam, and so you are clear to use them as superpowered distractions or unkillable meat shields if you wish. You don’t have to be as cowardly as we were, but if you have an hour free to watch an action movie scene play out while peeking out from behind the corner of a refrigerator, then that option is available to you. There are certainly quicker ways to reach GTA 6’s highest wanted level of six stars, which means you’ll be hunted down until you’re dead, but this is one of the safest and requires minimal munitions from your own stockpile. Early on, we opted for the plane crash onto a beach, before mowing down all of the vacationers in a truck method, but since then, millions of players have been finding their own road to infamy. But, in case you ever needed to know. Yes, it is possible to get six stars in GTA 6 with just a single bullet and grenade. As for just the single bullet itself… well, we’ll keep on trying. What have been your wildest six-star stories? Let us know in the comments! title: It Turns Out Jason Might Have a History With Mandy in GTA 6 After All

content: As soon as GTA 6 was in our hands, an early game character quickly became a fan favourite: Mandy. Warning! Spoilers for GTA 6 follow. It's not hard to see why. Fans then did a little digging and found out that Mandy is almost definitely hiding a dark secret ; she's probably killed people. That makes her advances towards Jason — like insisting they were supposed to be married — look dangerously delusional. Jason might have dodged a literal bullet. However, there is some easy-to-miss dialogue in GTA 6 that suggests Mandy wasn't basing her infatuation with Jason on nothing. You can come across this dialogue as soon as you take control of Lucia and find a meditation spot . The meditation sequence will play some audio from the character's past, usually centred around their insecurities. title: On Top of Everything Else, GTA 6 Is a Solid Stealth Sandbox
summary: I came to GTA 6 for its wild car chases and explosive shootouts, but its the really solid stealth that has me hooked.
content: This is an opinion piece from writer Samuel Horti. IGN's opinion columns represent the personal viewpoints of the writer, drawing on their own experiences and research to explore the exciting world of video games. Grand Theft Auto is a boisterous, brash series full of loud characters and louder explosions. GTA 6 continues that tradition for many of its main story beats, chaining showy set-pieces into lethal car chases, but in my 35 hours roaming Leonida I've found plenty of chances to engage with its surprisingly robust stealth system. In some cases, it even feels like Rockstar specifically designed areas with sneaking and silencers in mind. Illegal operations are lucrative robbery opportunities dotted around the map that hide cash, jewellery, drugs, and unique items – cars, weapons, watches – guarded by armies of enemies. I struggled with them early on: shooting my way to the valuables attracted GTA 6's menacing police, curtailing my heists before I could grab all the loot and forcing me to flee across entire counties while a chopper buzzed overhead. Now, I treat these scenarios like stealth vignettes, my goal to remain hidden for as long as possible. I've screwed silencers onto my weapons and prioritized headshot precision over spraying power, carrying a pistol alongside either a tactical rifle or a sniper. My shotgun is purely for backup, just in case. Skirting around these hideouts reveals hidden entrances. For Janjak's Garage in Vice City, for example, you can mantle a dumpster in a neighbouring alley to reach the garage's sheet metal roof. Out West, on the edge of Port Gellhorn, you can avoid the main gates of the giant Brooks Boatworks and slip through holes in the fence. Stealth detection is intuitive. Crouching reduces noise, sightlines feel realistic, and you'll be warned by a yellow arrow over an enemy's head before they fully spot you, allowing you a window to nip back into cover. Knives silently slice enemies' open or you can choke them quietly from behind. And if you need space, you can whistle from cover to draw foes over, or throw bottles to distract them. It's classic stealth game fare. But I've found that guns with silencers are actually the best option because they avoid the risk of an enemy spinning around at the wrong moment and catching you, knife raised. They mask shots almost completely: I've stood close to enemies and shot at others without being detected. Not everything in GTA 6 adopts Rockstar's general pursuit of realism. Illegal operations feel like the real test of your sneakiness, and I'm relishing each new one that pops up on my map. Clusters of enemies are tricky because as soon as you shoot one, the others will spin and look for you. Here, I use focus mode to slow time and pop a series of headshots, plink, plink, plink. Three bodies thud simultaneously. I feel like prime Sam Fisher. High ground is vital and from the right vantage I can survey the area, plan my route, and pick off enemies from distance. I always clamber to the loftiest point and use the D-pad to tag visible hostiles, which tracks them through walls. In a pinch, focus mode will highlight enemies through walls too, although only if they're nearby. Some of the level design feels like it's steering you down this silent route. Back at the Boatworks, the first thing I saw after sneaking in was a platform lift to the roof of the main warehouse, high above every enemy. A drop in the ceiling led me to an empty top floor – I've seen this trick repeated in other hideouts, so I always look for ladders or other ways to reach the roof. In the bigger compounds, staying silent for longer than a few minutes is a real challenge. No matter how many times I ran the Boatworks (I saved before I tried, and reloaded when I failed) I was always eventually spotted by some unaccounted-for enemy. But I reached a point where I could reliably clear the main warehouse floor-by-floor and empty the safe without anyone spotting me. That gave me a headstart on the police when I was eventually found, and by the time officers arrived I'd slipped back out through the fence, goodies jingling in my stash bag. This feels like the first time stealth has been a core part of a GTA game. During standard stick-ups of stores and jewellers you can find back entrances, kill the alarm and erase security tapes – but you'll always need to confront staff if you want to grab absolutely everything. For that reason, illegal operations feel like the real test of your sneakiness, and I'm relishing each new one that pops up on my map. They have the feel of Far Cry's outposts: flexible, self-contained diversions that I can tick off whenever I need more cash, or just fancy a change of pace. I've loved all my time with GTA 6 so far, but the best I've felt is when, this morning, I robbed Sound4Sound Studio in north Vice City. After hopping the fence I systematically cleared the parking lot and slipped inside, carving through the building, headshot after headshot. Nobody saw me coming, the police never arrived, and afterwards I could explore unchallenged, helping myself to every last bundle of cash. I drove off in a unique custom car, orange paint glistening, tens of thousands of dollars to the good. I'd take a whole game of these scenarios. Thankfully, I've still got 30 left. One final bonus of stealth: silencers are comically long, so now Lucia walks around Vice City carrying a gun taller than she is. title: Rockstar North Boss Knew Some GTA 6 Players Would 'Reject' New Systems Like Criminal Profiles, but Insists 'You Can Still Do Whatever You Wanted to Do Before'
summary: Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson knew some GTA 6 players would "reject" new systems like criminal profiles, but insisted "you can still do whatever you wanted to do before."
content: GTA 6 is by far the furthest Rockstar has pushed one of its games on a gameplay level. Perhaps nothing showcases that more than the criminal profile system ticking away in the background at all times, judging the way you act in its world as Jason and Lucia. No longer is Grand Theft Auto a sandbox where hedonism is widely encouraged, but a place that judges you for partaking in it. It’s a system that has caused much debate within the player base, with some feeling as if they’re being punished for how they traditionally played GTA games. It was something that Rockstar admitted to have been a little worried about when YouTuber TGG visited the studio months ago and claimed it was "going to change GTA." "I thought, 'Oh s**t, we’re in trouble,'" Rockstar co-studio head Rob Nelson told VGC . “But I said, 'It doesn’t change everything; it changes what GTA can be.' So for us, I think it opens a new range of choices and decisions for the player to make. You can still do whatever you wanted to do before, but now you have other options." Warning! Spoilers for GTA 6 follow. The criminal profile system reacts to how violently you choose to act throughout GTA 6’s open world and missions. Opt for headshot kills over debilitating kneecaps? You’ll move away from the "professional" end of the spectrum towards "psycho" and eventually "irredeemable." From experience, though, I can confirm that it takes quite the effort to reach that point on the scale after going on one murderous rampage after the next. Which criminal profile you land on by the end of Jason and Lucia’s story will factor into which ending you get, but for the most part, it’s not something that necessarily needs to be playing on your mind at all times. My characters were considered “professional” at the end of my playthrough, and, believe me, I spilt my fair share of blood along the way. Nelson appears to know that not all players will necessarily be on board with changes to the GTA formula like this, though, and expects some to "reject this new stuff we’re offering." He does hope it may help to make people think differently about how they approach Rockstar games in a post-Red Dead Redemption 2 world, though. "I hope it changes the way players who want to engage with it play the game," Nelson continued to tell VGC. "In GTA 5 you started with a bank robbery in North Yankton, and you’re murdering like 40 cops off the rip, and you’re setting these guys up as what they are. We were conscious of that. "Lucia takes the bullets out of the gun at the start of the game. She goes in, and it’s not like you can kill a bunch of people. So we wanted to start them off with a bit less baggage. They’re trying to make a go of this semi-legitimate life. When you pick up with Jason, he’s still a criminal; he’s still getting in trouble with Donnie and all that, but he’s sort of been living this relatively criminal-adjacent existence." Whether GTA 6 feels like "classic GTA" or not is certainly a conversation to be had, but there’s no denying that the opening hours of Rockstar’s latest connects you to its characters more convincingly than the series has done in the past. title: Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair Dev's Explanation for Skipping Xbox Sparks Backlash
summary: Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition developer Playtonic has come under fire from Xbox owners after it ruled out an Xbox Series X and S version of the rerelease.
content: Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition developer Playtonic has come under fire from Xbox owners after it ruled out an Xbox Series X and S version of the rerelease. In a statement published online, the UK studio said it had to prioritize the PlayStation 5 and Nintendo Switch 2 versions because the cost of bringing it to Xbox "just isn't viable for us at this time." The original game, released in 2018, launched on Xbox One at the same time as PlayStation 4 and Nintendo Switch. The next-gen upgrade hits PC, PS5, and Switch 2 only on December 15. "Unfortunately, we've had to prioritize our efforts given the technical challenges and costs presented in the creation of this updated version of the game and as a result, we are unable to commit to any additional platforms for the forseeable future," Playtonic said. "We understand the frustration felt by those of you who won't be able to access the Definnitive Edition at launch, but unfortunately the cost of bringing it to more platforms just isn't viable for us at this time. As a small team, we hope you guys can understand the challenges we face. Please know that this wasn't an easy decision to make, and we apologize to any of you affected by this. "We only wish things were different, and we value every single one of you and your feedback." Playtonic's statement is light on specifics, but most are reading between the lines here and assuming what the studio is saying here is that it weighed up how much it would cost to port the rerelease to Xbox Series X and S against its potential return, and found the numbers didn't add up. "This means the game didn’t do meaningful numbers on the Xbox. It doesn’t make any sense otherwise," one person suggested . "They could’ve just said the game sold bad on Xbox and they don’t have enough money or time to justify updating it," another said . Whatever the reason, Xbox fans certainly aren't happy. "Slap in the face to Xbox fans who’ve supported you from the beginning," one Xbox user said . "Will not support you any longer or buy any future Playtonic games if we’re not gonna be treated equally." "It's a free upgrade for a game we've already brought. The same as the other platforms but you are treating us poorly," another added . "So no we don't understand. No matter how you slice it, it's a **** you to Xbox buyers." "So... you can't afford to make a FREE upgrade for Xbox... but you could afford it for every other platform?" one person asked . "Well... won't be buying anything of yours from this point on. So there's even less money for you." "I could buy this game on PS5 or Switch but it’s clear you don’t want or deserve my support," another said.
